exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with progressive dyspnoea, leg swelling, and a blood pressure of 165/100 mmHg. What is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform a bedside cardiac ultrasound to assess ejection fraction and look for pericardial effusion because echo guides immediate management when echo is available, otherwise rely on clinical signs.

A patient with known rheumatic mitral stenosis develops fever and a new holosystolic murmur. Which condition must you exclude and what test confirms it? — Exclude infective endocarditis; obtain multiple blood cultures and a transthoracic echo if possible.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a young adult presents with chest pain and elevated troponin but no ECG changes. How do you differentiate myocarditis from myocardial infarction? — Correlate with recent malaria infection, look for diffuse ST changes, and use echocardiography for global hypokinesis; coronary angiography is rarely available.

A patient on long‑term thiazide therapy for hypertension develops gout. What alternative antihypertensive would you choose and why? — Switch to an ACE inhibitor; it lowers BP without raising uric acid and provides renal protection.

During a ward round you encounter a patient with sudden hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and JVD. What emergency management should you initiate? — Perform urgent pericardiocentesis if skilled, give IV fluids, and arrange immediate transfer for surgical drainage.

A 30‑year‑old HIV‑positive woman presents with pericardial effusion on ultrasound. Which anti‑TB regimen is recommended and what adjunctive therapy improves outcome? — Start standard 6‑month anti‑TB therapy plus a 6‑week course of oral prednisolone to reduce constrictive complications.
ai.title: Cardiovascular System Pathology
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A concise guide to common cardiovascular diseases in low‑resource settings, focusing on clinical reasoning, diagnosis, staging, and management without relying on unavailable tests.

b: Identify the organ system involved (heart, arteries, veins, pericardium).
Use WHO criteria for rheumatic heart disease, Framingham risk factors for atherosclerosis, and WHO hypertension thresholds.
sections.p: Cardiovascular pathology encompasses structural and functional disorders of the heart and vessels that cause morbidity or death. Diagnosis rests on history, physical exam, and targeted investigations.

b: NYHA I‑IV for heart failure.
Hypertension: Stage 1 (140‑159/90‑99 mmHg), Stage 2 (≥160/≥100 mmHg).
Rheumatic mitral stenosis: mild (MVA > 1.5 cm²), moderate (1.0‑1.5 cm²), severe (<1.0 cm²).
sections.p: Severity is graded by functional class (NYHA for heart failure), blood pressure stage, or anatomical classification (e.g., WHO/ISHLT for valvular disease).

b: Hypertension – leading cause of heart failure and stroke.
Rheumatic heart disease – common after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis.
Coronary artery disease – rising with urbanisation, diabetes, smoking.
Infective cardiomyopathy – HIV, TB pericarditis, malaria‑related myocarditis.
Sickle‑cell cardiomyopathy – chronic anemia and vaso‑occlusion.
sections.p: In East African hospitals the most frequent etiologies are hypertension, rheumatic heart disease, coronary artery disease, and infectious cardiomyopathies.

b: Sudden chest pain radiating to left arm – possible myocardial infarction.
Severe dyspnoea with orthopnoea – acute decompensated heart failure.
Fever, night sweats, pleuritic chest pain – tuberculous pericarditis.
New murmur with fever – infective endocarditis.
sections.p: Presentations vary from silent hypertension to acute chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, or peripheral oedema. Look for red‑flag symptoms that demand urgent care.
Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; when a test is unavailable, rely on bedside findings and basic labs.

t.b: Is the patient hypertensive? – confirms hypertension; guides treatment urgency.
Is there ischaemia or arrhythmia? – ST changes suggest MI; QRS abnormalities suggest hypertrophy.
Is there cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion? – Enlarged silhouette supports heart failure.
Is there pericardial effusion or reduced ejection fraction? – Visualizes fluid, wall motion; substitutes for echo if unavailable.
Is there anaemia, infection, or inflammation? – Low Hb worsens heart failure; high ESR supports rheumatic activity.
Are kidneys functioning? – Guides diuretic use and detects cardiorenal syndrome.

b: Pulseless electrical activity – cardiac arrest.
Cardiogenic shock – hypotension with cool extremities.
Tamponade signs – muffled heart sounds, JVD, hypotension.
Acute limb ischaemia – sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness.
sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening sequelae that require immediate intervention.

b: Hypertension – start ACE inhibitor or thiazide diuretic; avoid beta‑blockers in severe asthma.
Heart failure – loop diuretic for congestion, ACE inhibitor for remodeling; avoid NSAIDs which worsen fluid retention.
Rheumatic valve disease – secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks; surgery only when severe.
Acute coronary syndrome – give aspirin (if available) and refer for reperfusion; avoid fibrinolytics if contraindicated.
TB pericarditis – standard anti‑TB regimen plus corticosteroids; monitor for drug interactions.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve symptoms, and prevent progression. Use drug classes that are affordable and have a safety record in low‑resource settings.

b: BP check every 2 weeks until controlled, then monthly.
Weight log to detect early fluid gain.
Counsel on low‑salt diet, smoking cessation, and malaria prophylaxis where relevant.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce cardiac decompensation.
sections.p: Regular review of blood pressure, weight, and symptom burden; educate on lifestyle and adherence.

b: Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain; differentiate with clear lungs on X‑ray and risk factors.
Severe anemia – causes dyspnoea and tachycardia; check Hb.
Asthma exacerbation – wheeze and dyspnoea; bronchodilator response helps.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic cardiovascular disease in presentation.

b: Normal ECG does not exclude early myocardial infarction; repeat if symptoms persist.
Chest X‑ray may appear normal in early heart failure; rely on clinical signs.
ESR can be normal in chronic rheumatic disease; use clinical criteria.
sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.
